of affairs shall not continue any longer. Sometimes I ask myself just why we are here. We have a responsibility to those whom we represent. We all represent a great many of these unfortunate persons who were wounded during the war and I submit that we must rise in our places and make our position definite and clear no matter whom we may offend. Again I ask the minister to consider all the facts of this case. He is a sensible man, one of the best friends the soldiers of this country have ever had, and I am sure he will realize that this court of appeal is not functioning as it should.
I asked the minister the other night if he had any figures to show whether the number of first applications was diminishing or increasing.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have not the definite figures before me, but just before coming into the chamber I inquired of the pension commission and was told that for a while during the summer the number had increased, but it was becoming almost normal. There will be a slight decrease for the year.

Two years ago this parliament put a dead-line on first applications. The dead-line for those who served in England or Canada only was July 1, 1936, but for those who served in France it was extended to January 1, 1940. I suggest that that deadline should be extended for another two years. The new amendments are working satisfactorily, and there are still many men who received gunshot wounds but have not applied for pension. I suggest the minister give serious consideration to granting this extension.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is receiving consideration.

From what has been said this afternoon it would seem that members on all sides are in favour of granting some kind of pension to those who served in some capacity in the war or to their dependents. It has also been brought up by other hon. members that those who remained behind should receive some recompense. We have with us this afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Pensions and National Health, and it seems to me that these ministers should work together to solve this problem.
This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture said that he could not find a market for the cattle referred to by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson). The minister stated that there was a shortage of space in vessels going to Great Britain. We all know that

the tremendous surplus of wheat accumulated by the board of which Mr. McFarland was the head was sold at a loss to this country of over $2,000,000. Is that correct? We sell our wheat abroad at a loss; we find it impossible to find a market for our cattle, and yet we have all these people starving.
While I do not think the platitude about poverty in the midst of plenty should be referred to too often by members on this side of the chamber, at the same time there seems to be something anomalous in a situation which does not provide sufficient purchasing power to those who served with honour in the great war and their dependents. We feel that the different departments of the government should be able to solve this situation so that all people, including the returned soldiers-I have been a soldier but I did not serve in the great war-should have sufficient purchasing power. Why should we just worry about the widows and the orphans? We should consider all the people in Canada.
The Minister of Pensions and National Health says that these pensions cannot be granted because the Minister of Finance will not let him have the necessary money. He admits that the problem is practically unsolved. It seems to me that we should get together to consider the situation. We have this food and these cattle in abundance-I have a large number of cattle myself that I cannot get rid of at a profit if they are sold under the orthodox system of finance-and yet many people cannot purchase the necessities of life.
I trust that my remarks will not be considered as irrelevant. I simply state the situation as I see it. We hope that the government will do their best to solve this problem.

I thank my hon. friend for his suggestion. If only I could come to believe, or better still, if only I could get my colleague the Minister of Finance to believe, in the social credit theories, then all my difficulties would be washed away. All I would have to do would be to call upon the benighted treasury board and tell them to pay this or pay that and they would do it. Unfortunately I have to make arrangements to pay in real money. My hon. friends in the far comer may not have to do that, but I do. I must pay in the kind of money that everyone expects. I have not proceeded far enough in my financial studies to know whether or not it is good money; but I do know that the people to whom the Department of Pensions and National Health have to make payments want the kind of money the treasury board will issue, and not the kind of money my hon. friends would give us. If they can

settle that for me, I am quite willing to issue all the cheques necessary, or ask the treasury board to give me all the cheques that are requested.

I am very glad that the minister has made that remark, because our suggestion was that he pay in goods, and I am wagering that these widows would just as thankfully accept coal, flour, butter, eggs, cheese or a great many other things.
Where would you get the goods?
From the abundance in Canada.

Who has it? I would suggest that if my hon. friends possess such an abundance of goods as they so often speak of, they might give some of it to the people in their own province or anywhere else they happen to be who are in need.

speechtext: This discussion is entirely out of order.

I wish to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) that the deadline for applications for those who served in a theatre of war be extended to 1942. Formerly there was incorporated in the act a provision that if there was on record in the documents an injury, wound or disease due to service, it should be considered as an application; but that section has been deleted from the act. There is a large number of men who have not yet made application for various reasons, possibly because of an independence of spirit or because they are residing at some remote point. I know the minister will take every step necessary to protect their interests.
Perhaps I did not make myself clear to the minister the other evening in requesting information in regard to what extent the medical men under the jurisdiction of the Canadian pension commission have sanction to authorize treatment. May I ask this simple question: What authority, if any, has the pension commission to authorize treatment for pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I do not know just what
my hon. friend means. The pension authorities have their own medical men who are primarily pension medical officers, and they examine for pension. There are no longer any water-tight compartments. The two branches of the department were at one time, as my hon. friend knows, absolutely distinct and separate, and there was perhaps some confusion, but at the present time they are not separate. Perhaps the best instance I know of to give as an illustration is that in
Regina where, owing to the retirement of the district administrator there, Doctor Wick-wire, on account of age, the position of administrator was opened, and the pension doctor, a man formerly under the control of the pension commission, took his place, and so the two positions are now one. The man is at one and the same time a pension medical examiner and district administrator and chief medical officer. I think similiar conditions obtain pretty generally throughout the service.
I made some inquiries following my hon. friend's question the other evening, and I think I can state on the authority of both branches that there is no case of strife or dissension between the commission medical men proper and those engaged in treatment. There are occasionally matters of administrative detail which have to be worked out, but there is no conflict. I doubt very much whether we could ever go back to the system which existed prior to 1927 before the Scott report was made, when indiscriminately pension medical men and treatment doctors had the right to order men in or out of hospital, whereby almost endless confusion resulted, because it was impossible to make a proper check under those circumstances. Now that their work has been coordinated to the extent to which I believe it is I do not think there is any necessity of following any other procedure than that followed at the present time.
Is it the Regina case?

No; he is resident in
Seattle. He was discharged on January 14, 1918, as medically unfit. On enlistment he had operative scars resulting from varicose veins, both legs, which were not considered to be causing any disability at the time of enlistment. During service he was treated for dental caries, I.C.T. right foot, and neurasthenia. The medical board on February 1, 1917, reports the condition of shell shock, also hallux valgus. Pension is in effect for disability resulting from (1) neurasthenia, (2) varicose veins and (3) hallux valgus. The condition of neurasthenia is considered to have been incurred during service. The conditions of varicose veins and hallux valgus

are considered to be pre-enlistment conditions, obvious on enlistment, and aggravated one-fifth of the entire condition by service in France. Entire disability, forty per cent. Pensionable disability, sixteen per cent. That describes the condition of this pensioner.
On November 26, 1937, the United States Veterans' Administration in Seattle, Washington, reports that the pensioner has very marked varicose veins, left lower extremities, with a moderate amount of hallux valgus, and that surgical treatment is very necessary, and it is recommended.
On December 17, 1937, Doctor F. W. Blake-man, Department of Pensions and National Health, who, I understand, deals with all cases outside Canada, advised the United States Veterans' Administration as follows:
We have received the medical report of November 26, recommending operation for varicose veins. As this condition ante-dated enlistment, and as it was only aggravated to a very slight degree as a result of service, it is not considered that the extent of this aggravation is sufficient to warrant this department in undertaking any major treatment expenses. If, however, the condition can be treated by injection method at the out-patient clinic, we are prepared to authorize this form of treatment as a special consideration.
On January 5, 1938, the United States Veterans' Administration advises the Department of Pensions and National Health:
We have no facilities in this office for this type of treatment for such a severe degree of disability.
The point in this case is incorporated in this statement, and I wish to refer to one aspect of it, again in discussing the care of patients:
Following the refusal by the department to provide surgical treatment for the pensionable condition of the above named, the Canadian pension commission increased his pension on the grounds that his disability had increased.
I submit that that is a clear-cut case where it would be in the public interest as well as in the interest of the pensioner himself to grant treatment. As I understand the situation, the pension medical authorities have no power to do anything more than refer this case to the treatment branch, and they cannot recommend or authorize treatment.

This is the case of regimental No. 40686; private X; resident in Elgin, Ontario. He is in receipt of a pension at the rate of fifty per cent for pulmonary tuberculosis. I will not do that. I will give the hon. member the assurance that I will not, because it would be very bad administration; that is the principal reason. But in so far as telling every officer in the department, wherever he is, from the highest to the lowest, that there is to be "no chiselling on the soldiers," that was done the first time I came in. There is not going to be too much petting of them, nor will there be any chiselling anywhere.
The hon. member will recollect, if his memory takes him over the years as mine does, that all the way through it has been the habit to blame some one person or some one branch. At one time no member of parliament dare mention the pension commission in this chamber; if he did, immediately there was a storm. The pension commissioners, and particularly the chairman of the commission, were persons to be avoided. The chairman's name was not even respectable, and the very idea of that commission, or anyone having anything to do with pensions, looking after the treatment of the poor soldiers, would have raised a revolution in this house. That was only because for some reason or another the soldiers had taken an aversion to the personality of the man who was then in charge of pensions. At another time it was some other official. But in spite of the particular antipathy, rightly or wrongly, of certain hon. members or of certain soldier associations, the administration of the department must go on, and I cannot give the assurance to any hon. member that because he does not happen to like the colour of the hair of some of the doctors in my department I am going to change the whole system. That would be neither fair nor reasonable.
As I have said, in years gone by we got ourselves into endless difficulties by having two authorities having equal jurisdiction over the persons who were to be treated in our hospitals. It was found after the fullest investigation by an outside body, a firm of accountants and experts, that this system could not work, and the result was that we arrived at what we are doing now. I did not create what now exists; but I certainly would not like to bring about a kind of earthquake in the whole administration of the department, particularly when by good will and coordination we can get far better results, and I think that is what we are now getting.
As to the cases cited by the hon. member, let me say something which perhaps will not please some people. There has been a tendency, which I am trying to make disappear as far as the department is concerned, on the part of both the soldiers and the department to argue a case purely from the technical standpoint. They are chasing one another around by the tail. The house passes some piece of legislation with the laudable intention of bringing under the benefits of pension law or of treatment a particular class of people. Immediately others who are no more entitled to it than the man in the moon come in under it. The result is that in the minds of some of the officers there may be a hardening against people who take technical advantage of the act to obtain certain things.
One of the worst cases with reference to treatment, one that has given me the most trouble, is that of a man who, after having been discharged from the United States army because of tuberculosis, was three days in the Canadian army before he went to hospital, where he remained. We have spent $35,000 on him, and never a day passed but there were complaints from that man that he was not getting enough pay and allowances. He received pay and allowances from 1917 on. Very recently, unfortunately, he died. But that man continually bothered us and had half the returned soldier organizations in this country bothering us, trying to take advantage of some technical point that his disability was aggravated during the three days' service he had in the Canadian forces prior to being hospitalized.
Sometimes the soldiers go too far. If there has been any tendency in the department to resort to technicalities-a tendency which I hope and believe I have been able to check by constantly repeating that such is not the policy of the department-it has been to some extent the fault of those who endeavoured to take advantage of the legislation lo obtain for themselves benefits to which they were not entitled. If there are complaints from all

Supply-Pensions-European War
over the country-and I receive them, as no doubt every hon. member does-that certain people are drawing one hundred per cent pension to which they are not entitled, it is because of this very tendency; they have taken advantage, perhaps properly, of the act because possibly we have not given sufficient consideration to all the implications of the legislation we introduced.

I wish to make it clear that I am not animated by personal antagonism to any particular official of the department, nor am I directing this criticism to the minister. I see no reason why the minister should have entered into such an elaborate defence of his department. But in the last two years, from constant contact with a number of cases, I am convinced there have been definite indications of some tightening up in the application of regulations-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I deny that.

-by certain officials in the treatment branch. That is evident as you meet the men, not "lead swingers," who have been deprived of various attentions that they formerly received. I think I am competent to judge of a "lead swinger." I am here citing the cases of two men who gave evidence of making an effort to reestablish themselves; they desired treatment in order that they might carry on in their occupations rather than be wholly dependent on a pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I absolutely deny there has been any tightening up of the treatment regulations since I came into office. On the contrary, the hon. member will find that the system is as wide open as it can be; that instructions have been given everywhere, "The regulations are not there to keep people from getting treatment; they are there to enable them to get it." That is the theory on which the officers of my department are instructed to act.

I accept the minister's
assurance and I believe every hon. member knows that his attitude towards the problem has been as he has stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I resent the implication that since I came in we have tightened up. It is not true.

I withdraw any remark
of mine which leaves the inference that the minister has been in any way responsible. The minister must be aware, however, that at certain times officials in endeavouring to draw up regulations may lop off here and there, perhaps unjustly, men who should receive pension or treatment. When I men-

tioned that period I was not referring specifically to the time during which the department has been under the present minister. I am not developing an attack against the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I wish you were; there would be something to answer.

I am merely suggesting
that there should be a regulation whereby, when the pensions medical authority passes in favour of the pensioner, that judgment shall be acted upon without hesitation by the treatment branch. If the minister can give some assurance that this can be done-and I believe that he has the power to do so-the trouble in this regard will disappear immediately.

Is there any possibility of a pension being increased in a case of this kind? A man was given a pension of S17.25 a month, being then able to work. Subsequently he was unable to work and was advised that if it could be shown that he had a defective heart condition, further consideration would be given him. He was examined and was advised by the pension commission that there was no change in his pensionable condition since his previous examination, and under these circumstances no consideration could be given him. This man was unable to work; he is still not able to do anything. Is there any possibility of an increase in a case of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I assume it was decision of the pension commission, which alone has authority to assess and award or to refuse pensions.

We have had complaints about quorums of the commission taking the opinion of medical men who live in a different city from the applicant. For example, a man may appear before a quorum in Calgary and have medical evidence given there, but then his file is sent to a doctor in Toronto or Montreal for an opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I never thought that medical science was confined to one locality. If a man is a good doctor he is as capable of diagnosing diseases in Calgary as in Toronto. Perhaps, however, I misunderstand the hon. gentleman's statement.

The point is this, that the man is actually seen in person by the doctor in Calgary and not by the doctor in Montreal or Toronto as the case may be. I understand the departmental hospitals are all in large centres. Would it not be possible to have experts in the different cities pass upon these cases only after actually seeing the

Supply-Pensions-European War
applicants, instead of the quorums simply referring a man's file to a doctor in another city who has never seen the applicant? There is a good deal of complaint in that regard, and I am wondering whether it is not possible to alter the present method.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is a little difficult to bring every applicant who claims that he has a disability, from Calgary to Montreal or Toronto for examination by specialists there. It would be costly.
Could he not be examined by an expert in Calgary?

I wish to draw to the attention of the committee a certain case, not as an indvidual complaint but as representing the position of a considerable body of imperial war veterans in Canada. For the purpose I might read part of a letter I wrote to the chairman of the pension commission on October 30, 1937. I shall not mention the name. The letter refers to No. 510250 and reads:
I have had drawn to my attention the case of the above mentioned man, who is confined to the Mountain Sanatorium, Hamilton, Ontario, suffering from T.B.
He was an acting sergeant in the Army Service Corps, 3rd Divisional train for several years when through a shortage of officers in the artillery of the Imperial army, he joined that force and served in same for several years until gassed at the front. He served in the Imperial Army in the 168th Siege Battery 68th Brigade.
As you know, during the war, there was a certain amount of encouragement offered capable men in the Canadian ranks to join and take out a commission in the Imperials. This encouragement being of course on solely patriotic grounds. I feel, however, that there is some weight to my argument that while this man was gassed while in the Imperial forces, he left Canada in the Canadian ranks and is, in my opinion, a responsibility of the Canadian government.
Two days later I received from General McDonald a letter in reply in which he said that under the Pension Act nothing could be done. He suggested, however, that this man might apply under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. Unfortunately the man died four days after, though that is not the point. What I w'ant to emphasize is this. If a man leaves Canada in the Canadian forces and is allowed to transfer to another unit, our responsibility to him as Canadians does not cease.

I wish to direct the attention of the minister to the neurological cases. The situation that existed and tvas discussed in 1936 has not improved; in fact it is getting worse. I would ask that these men receive the protection originally intended by parliament under section 11, subsection 1 (b) of the Pension Act, which reads:
No deduction shall be made from the degree of actual disability of any member of the forces who has served in a theatre of actual war on account of any disability or disabling condition which existed in him at the time at which he became a member of the forces; but no pension shall be paid for a disability or disabling condition which at such time was wilfully concealed, was obvious, was not of a nature to cause rejection from service, or was a congenital defect.
The amendment, for which I hope to get the approval of the minister, is that after the words "congenital defect," there be added the words "of a nature other than mental, psychopathic or neuropathic." The interpretation placed upon the words "congenital defect" results in great injustice to those who suffer from certain types of mental or nervous disease. The problem has appreciable proportions; there are 4,500 suffering from nervous diseases, and possibly a large percentage of these would come under this particular section.
I shall not attempt to argue with the doc-' tors. I know that many eminent members of the medical profession have expressed opinions on this matter, but it is far more important to look at it from a common sense point of view and particularly in the light of the original intention of parliament. When you consider the history of the Pension Act, it was clearly the intention of parliament to pension for the entire disability apparent in a man at the time of his discharge, provided that any pre-enlistment condition was not obvious or wilfully concealed. The words " or was a congenital defect" were added subsequently to 1918 or 1919, but clearly for the purpose of dealing with such defects as a bodily deformity which perhaps was not apparent at first. It was never the intention of parliament to deprive those suffering from nervous or mental disease of the protection which this section affords. I might refer to some important statements made in days gone by with respect to the intention of this section. The Hon. Mr. Rowell, chairman of the parliamentary committee in 1919. made a statement in the house. The statement is reported in Hansard of 1919 at page 4174 and is as follows:
If a man reached France, then he gets a pension, regardless of any pre-existing disability. That is the law as it stands in the pension regulations.
Again, discussing the report of the committee he said, as reported at page 4176 of Hansard of the same year:
But the committee thought, if the army medical service passed a man through and he

Supply-Pensions-European War
actually got to the front, we should ignore any question of pre-existing disability and grant him a pension.
Mr. Archibald, then legal adviser of the board, made this statement:
Those who got to France are pensionable for any disability which exists in them at the time of discharge unless the disability was obvious or concealed on enlistment.
And he goes on at length to present the argument, concluding with these words:
The parliamentary committee of 1918 came to tlie conclusion that if any man reached a theatre of actual war it must be definitely presumed that he was absolutely fit upon enlistment unless it could be proved that there was a pre-enlistment disability which was concealed or was obvious, or was of so minor a nature as not to cause rejection from service.
In 1922 the pension board gave effect to a memorandum which became famous at that time. Paragraph B stated:
That in any case previously fully pensionably under section 25 (3) -
Now referred to as section 11 (b).
-and in which it is decided that aggravation on service lias ceased, further pension cannot be awarded after the aggravation is deemed to have disappeared.
That was dealt with by the Ralston commission, which reported as follows:
(b) The commission is further of the opinion that, in view of the circumstances hereinbefore set out as to the application of section B of the minute of September 29, 1921, all cases within the provisions of section 25 (3) in which pension has been discontinued on the ground that aggravation or increase of disability on service has ceased or disappeared, should be reviewed and adjusted on the basis of the ruling contained in the general instruction of June 26, 1922.
Appropriate action was taken subsequently by parliament and we have the present section 11 of the Pension Act.
Now the chief neuropsychiatrist of the department prior to the parliamentary committee of 1936 reviewed a number of these cases. I shall not go into the evidence taken on that occasion except to say that any change of diagnosis in anj' of these cases affected the decision of the pension commission. Apparently he made an attempt to review and analyse the files a little more closely, for the purpose, he said, of constructive treatment. Here, again, I am not questioning the professional status of this medical gentleman; but he does say with reference to men incapacitated to-day as a result of mental or nervous disorders, designated neurological or psychoneurotic cases or whatever the term may be, that in the majority of these cases the disabilities were of constitutional origin. He claimed that a man had a psychopathic per-

sonality of constitutional origin; that a neurosis, probably anxiety neurosis, was superimposed on that mental defect during service, and that subsequent to service this had subsided, or if still in existence was due to economic conditions or worry. Therefore entitlement would be admitted only in respect of the neurosis or what might remain in consequence of neurosis, but no consideration could be given under the Pension Act to the pre-existing psychopathic condition or mental defect which he contended was of constitutional origin. That results in depriving all these men of the protection designed for them by parliament as far back as 1918 and 1919.
To all intents and purposes this man was fit on enlistment, if any mental defect existed in him at that time, even though of constitutional origin, it did not deprive him of ability to carry on in his occupation or to serve effectively in France, nor was it apparent to anyone. As far as evidence goes in the majority of these cases, the man carried on in normal fashion, discharged the ordinary duties of life and the duties required of him in the army effectively until the break-down. The neurosis, or mental or nervous breakdown, or whatever term may be used, was the last straw, was the disturbing factor which resulted in a break-down. The very fact that they admit the presence of that neurosis is in my opinion admission of a very definite aggravation. As a layman I cannot see how it is possible to draw the line between the pre-existing psychopathic condition, if it did exist prior to enlistment, and the neurosis. Certainly, in combining the two, the result is almost disastrous to such a man. We have them in large numbers of cases to-day wholly incapacitated as a result of that experience in service. I consider that attempting to delve into the pre-enlistment history is grossly unfair and unjust. In the cases I have had opportunity to examine there is no evidence of pre-enlistment condition. The opinion ventured by the chief neuropsychiatrist of the department is based on medical theory; and, as they admit themselves, the science is not exact by any means. These decisions are hair-splitting and based on fine-spun medical theory alone.
As I see it, there is only one way now of extending to these men the protection originally intended by parliament, that is by a definite amendment to the act such as I have suggested. I think the minister is right in suggesting that no good purpose could be served by attacking the medical officer in question, though I disagree with him on his findings. I am well aware that a board of consultants brought down an opinion more or less upholding his views; but I point out

_________ Supply-Pensions-European War
that the doctor himself went on the stand and said he was approaching the problem from the point of view of constructive treatment, and I have not yet discovered that it has taken fully into consideration the consequences of that change of diagnosis when that opinion is passed on to the pension commission.
It may be said to the credit of the chairman of the pension commission that he has carried on attempting to administer justice in the majority of these cases with very little change of policy; nevertheless the situation of many of these men at the present time is precarious. 1 am well aware that the chief neuropsychiatrist is an official of the treatment branch and that the pension commission is under no obligation to accept his opinion; nevertheless when a man of his professional status does place on file a finding or diagnosis as I have described, and uses the term "of constitutional origin," that must of necessity influence the opinion of the medical men on the pension commission. It is held as being synonymous with the term "congenital defect". That interpretation of this section, in the light of the medical evidence and medical opinion expressed, is as I say depriving several thousand ex-service men of the protection originally intended under the section which I have quoted. I hope the minister will take the earliest opportunity to open this subject up by way of amendment to the act and make very clear that pre-enlistment conditions of this nature are not considered in regard to pensions in connection with those who served in a theatre of actual war.
I understood the minister to say a little while ago that he would like to give the committee a decision on the question of widows' pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No, I did not. I am giving an opinion.
Well, would it not be possible to place that opinion before this committee at this session?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I hardly think so.
Would it be possible for further negotiation to take place between the governments regarding the problems of exservice imperials at present in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have no objection to taking part in any negotiations. I would not mind a trip to Europe if the government is willing to send me to negotiate, but I do not know what I could say to them more than I have already said.
Will the minister explain the decrease in this vote this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Based on the figures covering the operations of the Canadian pension commission over a period of nine months, I anticipate that the total amounts paid out in respect of European war pensions which, for the fiscal year 1936-37 amounted to $41,424,432.74, will, during the current fiscal year, show a reduction in the vicinity of $600,000. In that year $40,330,000 comprised the regular monthly payments made to pensioners. This amount will show during the current year a net decrease of about $130,000.
There are many factors and activities which produce variations both up and down in these amounts, but by far the major influences leading to decreases are the deaths of pensioners and the discontinuation of additional allowances to children on their reaching the age limit for pension-sixteen in the case of boys and seventeen in the case of girls. On the other hand, the amounts are increased by new awards of pension; by the extension of additional allowances to children beyond the age limit, who are continuing at school and whose parents are in necessitous circumstances, and by the increase in the rate of pension to existing pensioners whose disabilities are causing them greater handicap as the years go by. Other factors of a minor nature enter into the financial picture, but are not of any considerable moment in the aggregate.
Deaths of pensioners are providing a reduction of approximately $750,000, and the discontinuance of children's allowances, less the amount allowed for extension beyond the age limit, will account for about $480,000. These are the major factors on the decrease side.
On the other hand, new awards of pension, both to ex-soldiers themselves, who receive' entitlement, and to widows and dependents of Jhose who die, will amount to about $535,000, and the increased pension due to higher percentages being paid will add another $540,000. Other major factors which will have the effect of reducing the amount are the sums involved in what are described as first payments and retroactive payments. These are non-recurring payments which cover back periods for which pensioners are entitled to payments under the provisions of the act. In 1936-37 these payments accounted for $938,000. Largely due to the limitations on such payments provided for in the amending legislation of the session of 1936, during the present year these sums will show a very considerable reduction, and will not amount to more than $450,000, making a reduction under these items alone of nearlv half a million dollars.



Supply-Pensions-European War
In regard to actual numbers, new awards to disability pensioners have been slightly greater than the numbers of deaths and discontinuations. As at December 31 last there was a total of 79,881 disability pensions and 18,122 dependent pensions, a total of 98,003, involving an annual liability of $40,589,757.
Is it expected there will be a decrease each year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I cannot say; I do not know. It is likely, but probably not so substantial.
In view of the different points which have been raised throughout the discussion of the item, would it be possible to have amendments made to the Pension Act at this session?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member would expect me to tell him about any legislation at this time. For the moment I am considering whether I shall bring in legislation dealing with the Pension Act. So far no decision has been reached. That is the best answer I can give.

I do not wish to weary the minister and members of the committee; but as the minister has said, this is our one opportunity of advancing suggestions with respect to amendments to the act. I would suggest that if the minister is considering amendments he might consider the deletion of section 77. This section reads:
Notwithstanding anything contained in this or any other act, no pension, or additional pension, awardable or payable under the provisions of this act, shall be awarded or paid,
(a)	under schedule A or schedule B of this act, to or in respect of any child of a member of the forces or pensioner, if such child shall have been born on or after the first day of May, 1933;
(b)	under schedule A of this act, to or in respect of the wife of a member of the forces or pensioner, if she shall have been married to him on or after the date aforementioned-
And so on. I think all hon. members clearly understand that this section was introduced as a measure of economy and at a time when national revenues were at a low ebb. According to statements by the government, that condition no longer persists. They say we are well on the way to economic recovery, and I think we may well do as has been done in Australia, namely, restore benefits formerly taken away because of economic pressure.
Under subsection (a) of this section a very curious situation arises. Two of the children of a pensioner may be receiving a pension,

but two of them born subsequent to May, 1933, may not receive a pension. This is a difficult situation to explain. Furthermore, with regard to wives who marry subsequently -say in 1932-it is becoming extremely difficult to explain to them why, even if a husband dies from disability held to be attributable to war service, a pension is not awarded. Many rather unfair anomalies exist, and I would ask the minister to take the matter into consideration when he has in mind amendments to the Pension Act, or if he decides to bring the act under review this session.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Carried?
As the item is not carried, there are a number of other suggestions. The item is not carried, is it? I have other suggestions to make.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The debate on it is closed, if it is carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have no objection to permitting it to stand. We shall have to have another two hour sitting at some other time, with respect to the same item. If the item were passed, I should be very grateful to the hon. member; but if he does not wish it to pass, there is nothing I can say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I asked if it carried, and no one said anything. I assumed that it had.
Two members were on their feet.
Would the minister permit discussion of one or two points on another vote? If he would do that, we could pass it this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I should be very glad to do that. I endeavoured the first night to limit discussion to the single item. Since then the freest discussion has been carried on, but I confess I was not very successful in my attempts to control the committee. It can run as wild as it likes now.
We would like to help the minister, if he would agree to the discussion of pensions on another item.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There will be an item under the administration of the whole department, and there will be nothing to prevent an hon. member from making any suggestion he wishes at that time.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

Niagara Falls Observation Bridge
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. A. B. DAMUDE (Welland) moved the second reading of Bill No. 15, to incorporate Niagara Falls Observation Bridge Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it will be necessary for me to make any extended remarks at this time in connection with this bill. This is a bill to incorporate the Niagara Falls Observation Bridge Company which is to erect a bridge between Niagara Falls, Ontario, and Niagara Falls, New York. It is felt that this bridge will be very much in the interests of the public at this particular time.

I notice by the newspapers that it is the intention of the Ontario government also to erect a bridge. May I ask the hon. member if the Ontario government have expressed any wishes in regard to the present bill?
To the best of my knowledge this bill is in accordance with the wishes of the Ontario government and the Niagara Falls park commission.

I may not be in order in asking this question, but I notice from the papers that one of the promoters of this com-,pany is related to one of the commissioners of the Niagara Falls park commission and another is related to the Minister of Highways of Ontario. If this report in the papers is correct, it does not seem quite right to me that this bill should go through.
I think the statement with respect to the first gentleman is correct.
Which one is that?
The brother of a park commissioner, Mr. Kaumeyer, is named in the bill. There appears in the bill no blood relation^ of the Minister of Highways of Ontario, but his law partner is mentioned.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

subtopic: PENALTY FOR DIRECTORS AND OFFICERS PERMITTING VIOLATION OF THE ACT

speechtext:
Mr. H. E. BRUNELLE (Champlain) moved the second reading of Bill No. 13, to amend the Lord's Day Act.
He said: This amendment to the Lord's Day Act is intended to bring about a better 51952-531
observance of one of the ten commandments, namely, the one that says, "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." I do not think I need say very much about this bill to hon. members as I have often noticed the atmosphere of piety that falls over the house when you, Mr. Speaker, lead us in prayer at the opening of our daily sittings. I am sure that this bill will meet with the approval of the house.
It has often been said that corporations have no heart.. Two centuries ago Sir Edward Coke, who had much to do with the development of the law concerning joint stock companies, said that a corporation cannot commit treason, nor can it be excommunicated; for it has no soul. Hence the behaviour of corporations must be regulated by law. Certain works of necessity or of mercy are permitted to be done on Sunday, and it is not my intention to restrict the list of exceptions now given in the act.
Regretful as it may be, the fact is that certain corporations in the province of Quebec have been violating the provisions of the Lord's Day Act. Before saying anything further, let me comment on the fact that the directorates of these corporations are made up of all nationalities. There are French Canadians, English Canadians and American Canadians, probably in greater number, on these directorates. Our clergy have conducted a most strenuous campaign against these violations and complaints have been made by all classes in all communities without avail.
Our failure to put an end to these violations of the Lord's Day Act is evidently due in part to the fact that the penalties now provided are not severe enough and also to the fact that our working men or labourers are not sufficiently organized to resist the unlawful commands of their employers. Be it as it may, one must come to the conclusion that the penalties provided by the act have not been a sufficient deterrent. Section 14 of the act reads as follows:
Every corporation which authorizes, directs or permits its employees to carry on any part oi the business of such corporation in violation ot any of the provisions of this act, shall be liable, on summary conviction before two justices of the peace, for the first offence, to a penalty not exceeding two hundred and fifty dollars and not less than fifty dollars, and, for each subsequent offence, to a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars and not less than one hundred dollars, m addition to any other penalty prescribed by law for the same offence.
The amended section will read as follows:
Any person, being a director, an officer, a superintendent or an employee of a corporation, to whose direction or orders any employee is by the terms or conditions of his employment
Lord's Day Act

bound to conform, who authorizes, directs or permits any such last mentioned employee of that corporation to carry on any part of the business of the corporation in violation of any of the provisions of this act, shall be liable, on summary conviction before two justices ot the peace, to the same penalties as those to which a corporation is liable under subsection one of this section or, for a first oltence, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months and not less than one month, with or without hard labour, and for each subsequent offence, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months and not less than two months, with or without hard labour.
It will not be necessary to impose the gaol sentence as this will be discretionary. Many corporations have been prosecuted repeatedly, but when that happens, there is always delay in the proceedings. They have the money to go to appeal or even to pay a fine if necessary; but quite often, during and after the proceedings, the same violations are carried on. Much repair work is done on Sundays that could well be carried on during the week.
It is manifest that these corporations find it profitable to pay	a fine and	then	continue
to violate the law.
Who would object to this amendment? Corporations which are observing the law will not object. I take this opportunity to congratulate the directors of such corporations upon showing the same Christian spirit in the conduct of their	business as	they	show	intheir personal and private affairs. On the other hand, can it be said that the intended amendment is too drastic? In that case the objectors would	be either those	who	are
violating the law or those who intend to violate it. In neither case, I submit, are they entitled to sympathy or consideration.
Now, let us view this matter in the light of the 'sanctions imposed by our laws against those who violate the commandments of the decalogue, from	which our	law	for	the
observance of Sunday is derived. Most of the sections of our criminal code having their source in a moral obligation to do or not to do certain things provide for the imprisonment of those who violate the code. Here are a few examples.	.
"Thou shalt not kill." The violation of the section of our criminal code which is based on this commandment makes the offender liable to hanging, and, in the case of manslaughter, to imprisonment for life, and very few find fault with that penalty as being too extreme [DOT]
"Thou shalt not steal." The section of our criminal code which is based on this commandment makes the offender liable to imprisonment for a maximum of fourteen years, and I do not think the penalty is considered excessive, except perhaps by the offenders themselves.
{Mr. Brunelle.]
"Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife." It might be well for me not to make any comment on this commandment, particularly in the presence of bachelor members of the house, knowing not the tree of knowledge of good and evil, and who upon hearing some suggestion of matrimonial miseries might be forever scared away from the state of marriage ; so I will pass on.
Now the commandment upon which the Lord's Day Act is based reads thus: "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy." Here is a message from the Holy Book in reference to the penalty to be imposed upon those who do not observe the Sabbath day:
Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day there shall be to you an holy (lay, a sabbath of rest to the Lord.
And, sir, note this:
Whosoever shall do work therein shall be put to death.
My amendment to the Lord's Day Act does not go as far as that. I want the directois of corporations to live, but should they not let others live up to their religious convictions?
1 have shown, Mr. Speaker, that the Lord s Day Act is ineffective in many eases inasmuch as certain corporations find it profitable and advantageous to pay the fine and keep on violating the law. I have also shown that, relying on the unquestionable authority and wisdom of the Holy Scriptures, this house, will be amply justified in making the penalty for violation of the Lord's Day Act more severe in order to give the offenders the precious advantage of repenting at leisure in gaol for a short time at least.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I make a confident appeal to the good will of every member of the house, and particularly to the high moral and Christian character of the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to accept this amendment, and by so doing the house will have taken a most salutary step towards the enforcement of a law which is based upon the well-known and accepted precept not only of Christianity but of all known religions of the world, that one day of the week must be a day of rest.

Mr. Speaker, listening to
my hon. friend (Mr. Brunelle) I could not help remembering the circumstances under which this act was placed on the statute book. At that time members from my own province were not very keen on the enactment of the Lord's Day Act, and quite an agitation was carried on against it. I remember Mr. Bourassa and my friend Mr. Lavergne holding meetings of protest in the province

Lord's Day Act

of Quebec against this encroachment on the liberty of the subject, and there were quite a number of members on our own side of the house who spoke against the measure, but finally it was enacted. It is interesting to observe that to-day it is a member from the province of Quebec who proposes that the law shall be made stricter at least in one particular.
When my hon. friend introduced a similar bill last year I gave consideration to it. and had the bill come up for second reading I would have supported it. I have no reason to-day to change my attitude. There is no doubt that in the province of Quebec-I do not know whether it is the same in the other provinces-this law' has not been observed by certain big corporations as well as it should have been, and labour unions have been protesting strongly against violations of the law and asking that some amendment should be made. When proceedings are taken in the courts against offenders-and it is the attorney general of the province who has to authorize the issuing of proceedings before the courts- a corporation, when it is fined, pays the fine, and that is all there is to it. My hon. friend seeks to make the managers, the men who are in charge of the concern, responsible as well and to subject them to fine and imprisonment, to which the corporation is not subject.
There is one change I would suggest in the wording of the amendment. My hon. friend uses the words "the same" penalties. I think that would be equivocal, because it might mean one penalty payable either by the corporation or by the directors or the managers, and when the bill is in committee I shall suggest that the word "similar" be substituted for the words "the same," so that there will be no doubt that it will hit both the corporation and the directors or managers.
I congratulate my hon. friend upon having taken the initiative in this matter. I may say that the government was to move some amendments in order to meet the wishes especially of the labour unions, and of all citizens who desire that the Lord's Day be observed as it should be.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Woodsworth for the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the criminal code.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Since the house is in such an agreeable mood to-night, I hope that it will give favourable consideration to this bill, which seeks to guarantee labour the right to organize. When I was interrupted by the "nine o'clock" the other evening, I was pointing out that the trades unions have been urging legislation along this line. The follow-

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
mg resolution is rather typical of a number that have come to me. The chairman of the Toronto and district joint board of A.A. lodges, after certain of their officials had been dismissed because of their having joined a labour union, passed this resolution:
That the Toronto and district joint board of A.A. lodges, representing 2,500 steelworkers in the city of Toronto, most strongly urge upon the federal government the enactment of Bill 62-
That was the number by which the bill was known last year.
-thereby safeguarding our democratic rights as Canadian citizens and providing penalties for employers who would violate these rights.
This right to organize is being claimed not only by industrial workers but by members of professional organizations. I will read certain excerpts from a letter which I have received from the president of the Newspaper Guild of Montreal.
The Montreal Newspaper Guild was chartered in April, 1937, as a local of the American Newspaper Guild, an international union chartered by the American Federation of Labor. The American Newspaper Guild last June at its convention voted to affiliate with the Committee for Industrial Organization, and this decision of the convention was subsequently sustained by a referendum vote of the international membership. The other Canadian local of the guild was chartered in Toronto in the fall of 1936.
A little later:
On June 23, a number of members of the editorial staff of the Gazette were warned by the managing editor that they were jeopardizing their jobs by joining or retaining membership in the guild. Later that day I was discharged by the managing editor, who told me he had not been empowered to give me a reason for my dismissal. ... I had been employed by the Gazette for nine and a half years, and at the time of my discharge was assistant telegraph editor. I was then and still am president of the guild and represented the organization at the A.N.G.'s convention in June at St. Louis, Missouri.
It seems to me intolerable that men who attempt to join a labour organization or a professional organization should be intimidated and dismissed for no other reason than that they are members of those organizations. That is the reason for the introduction of the bill.
While it is true that matters of property and civil rights in the provinces-and I emphasize that phrase-come under provincial jurisdiction, I would point out that this is not a matter of a merely local or private nature. It is much wider than that, and hence it seems to me it might very well come under federal jurisdiction. I might point out, for example, that the solemnization of marriage

in the province is provincial but marriage and divorce are federal-British North America Act, section 91, item 26. The criminal law is federal, and there would seem to be no real reason why the refusal of an employer to grant what seems to us to be the legitimate rights of the workers should not be made a crime. Within the last few minutes we have undertaken to prevent employers from forcing men to work on the Lord's day. Why should not this much more important question be given favourable consideration?
The criminal code has a number of sections dealing with restraint of trade, the breaking of contracts, and so on. Trade unions were once considered illegal. Now they are especially exempted under section 498, subsection 2. Well, it would seem to me as a layman that if it is proper to put this sort of thing in the criminal code at one time, and later to make special exemptions, the whole subject'is one which naturally might come within federal jurisdiction under the criminal code. I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that it is quite proper that my amendment should find a place in the criminal code.
As one looks over the legislation of Canada and of most countries, one finds that there is one law for the employer and another law for the employee. The minister shakes his head.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: Surely it is not a crime for an employee to refuse to work for a certain employer?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
There is a very
great difference, as I shall proceed to point out. In many respects the employers are protected. This is the parallel: The employers have the right to organize and they are protected by charters; we ask simply that the employees should be given the right to organize-the right already enjoyed by the employers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
They
have it.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Oh, no. As we go back over British history we find that the nobles once ruled, and the laws in those days reflected very largely the interests of the nobles. The commons gradually gained power, and we find changes taking place in the law. Gradually there was the extension of the franchise. In the old days the franchise was very much limited, limited to employers, to men of substance, men of a certain class. Later on the franchise was extended so th?.t the employees, the poor people and finally all people obtained it. It was only within

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
comparatively recent years that labour had distinct representation in the House of Commons in Great Britain. Then certain more liberal or progressive laws were brought into force. Even the criminal code began to be altered not only because of the pressure of labour members in the House of Commons but because of enfranchised labour people throughout the country.
We in Canada have inherited to a very considerable extent the laws of Great Britain, many of them drawn up years and years ago, and our Canadian laws in many respects are those of Great Britain in the days before they had been modified, as they have been in England, under pressure of the growing labour forces. In Canada labour has had comparatively little political power, or, for that matter, economic power; otherwise we might have had more political power.
I would suggest that the laws on our statute books to-day are largely laws based upon an outgrown type of industry. In the old days there was the individual employer on one side and on the other the individual employee. As I illustrated the other evening, we sometimes still see the old arrangement in a simple shoemaker's shop-the employer on one side of the bench and the employee on the other side. Practically the two men are of equal bargaining power. But in the typical workshop to-day, behind the employer or the manager, stands a strong corporation, possibly a great group of corporations. What chance has the individual workman in bargaining with a corporation financed by millions? The situation is an impossible one. This condition made necessary the formation of trade unions. Originally, these were regarded as illegal in that they interfered with freedom of trade. To-day, however, trade unions are recognized; they are no longer illegal. But legislation has not gone so far as to make it possible for men to join trade unions without being discriminated against or dismissed.
Let me point out that to-day property is well protected, as it has always been. It is illegal for a man to break a piece of machinery, but there is no law against an employer dismissing a man or taking other action that might lead to the breaking lip of a home. I hope the Minister of Justice can see the close parallel that prevails there. A man can be dismissed and his dismissal may mean that he is permanently out of a job. It may be that he has no other economic resources and that may easily involve the breaking up of his home. There is absolutely nothing to protect the workman in these cases. But let a man injure in the slightest way a piece of machinery and immediately he is
haled before the courts. He is guilty. There is no equal protection. There is one law distinctly for the employer in the protection of his property and an altogether different law or no law when it comes to the protection of the worker in his job, which often is the only thing he has.
I urge that whoever controls a man's job under modem conditions controls his very life. I wonder whether those of us who work in this comfortable house, in these comfortable surroundings, for some months on end quite realize what it is to be out of a job and without the chance of getting another. Under modem conditions, the man who controls my job controls my very life, yet it would appear, according to our laws, that a man has no rights whatever to his job. He may be dismissed in the most arbitrary manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: Would you make it criminal for your electors to take away your job?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
No; that is another matter. I would make it criminal for them to take it away by some of the means used to-day, that is, bribery and intimidation; and that is what I want to prevent in this case.
To get back to this bill, I would suggest that organized employers to-day, incorporated and so on, are many of them denying to employees the rights which they themselves claim. Employers come here for charters, receive incorporation which gives them great power which they often exercise arbitrarily and without regard to the welfare of the employees. They are well protected; all this bill is designed to accomplish is that the employees, the labour people, are also protected. It is a different type of protection they need, but it is protection just the same, and protection which ought to be given.
I would make my appeal for the passage of this measure really on two grounds: first, there is the inherent right of freedom, freedom of speech, freedom of the press and freedom of organization.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: Of association.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Of association, if you will. We who come of British stock and have been nurtured in British traditions have always thought that Britishers ought to enjoy that freedom, but in practice we are very far from enjoying it. It is not sufficient to have what is called political freedom, the right to vote. It is not sufficient to have the right to travel up and down the king's highway. In order to enjoy complete freedom a man must have economic freedom. There is no use in saying. "I have the right to travel on the
Criminal Code

Trade Unions

railroad," unless I have something in the way of money in my pocket to enable me to travel. That is the important thing, and it is dependent on a measure of economic independence. To-day, if a man is to have freedom of association with his fellow workmen, he has to have some sort of economic security. That economic security can be swept away by the ukase of his employers.
This bill relates to the refusal of employers to recognize a trade union, or the intimidation of workers. I recall a rather celebrated case in the west in which one of the judges made a very strong statement with regard to the dangers of intimidation. This statement is taken from the charge to the jury of Judge Metcalfe in the King v. R. B. Russell. The judge said:
There is no right in this country under our laws so sacred as the right of personal liberty. No right of labour or capital, about which there has been so much declamation, is so sacred or so carefully guarded by the law of the land as is that of personal liberty. But personal liberty is not liberty of the body only. It is also liberty of the mind and will; and the liberty of a man's mind and will to say how he will bestow himself and his means, his talents and his industry. This is as much a subject of the law's protection as is that of his body. . . .
Take it from me, in strikes you can incite terror without hitting a man over the head. You can incite terror of starvation; you can incite terror of thirst. Is that not quite as effective as inciting by bodily violence? Your stomach will bring you quicker than a crack on the head sometimes. . . .
In this instance I quite agree with what Judge Metcalfe said. He made this charge to the jury with the idea of pointing out how dangerous it was for strikers to practise intimidation, but surely the principle is the same, precisely the same in the case of the employer. If employers intimidate, threaten to dismiss a man, that intimidation, according to Judge Metcalfe, is just as much an invasion of his liberty as if the man were hit over the head. I am inclined to think that we have minimized altogether too much this aspect of the matter, and have allowed men in authority, such as employers, to threaten. As I said a few minutes ago, if an employee breaks a piece of machinery he is under the penalty of the law. An employer who dismisses or threatens to dismiss a man for no other reason than that he belongs to a trade union is guilty of intimidation, which ought not to be permitted. If the intimidation were on the other foot, as it were, it would be prevented by the law.
I come back to the explanatory note appended to the bill. I would ask hon. members to give consideration to this, because it seems to me eminently fair:

The purpose of this bill is to prevent employers from refusing to employ, or from dismissing employees, or conspiring with others therefor, for the reason that they are members of a trade union.
As it is lawful for workmen or employees to form themselves into trade unions and to bargain collectively, it should, as a matter of public policy, be unlawful for employers to seek by overt acts or intimidation, threats or conspiracy to prevent them from belonging to such trade unions.
I hope that in considering this bill hon. members will recall that we are not living under conditions which prevailed one hundred years ago; we are living under modern industrial conditions. We are not living in an age v. hen labour was considered to have very few rights, as then labour had very little power either economically or politically. More than that, I would ask the members to consider that it is definitely in the public interest that we should not allow reactionaries in our midst to indulge in practices which almost inevitably lead to strife and bitterness and often to riots. Some blame the men who in desperation go on strike; blame rather the employers who refuse to recognize the unions which, for their protection and interests, the men are seeking to form.

friend refers to the Trades and Labour Congress. I am not talking; it is the Trades and Labour Congress that is talking.
-legislative competence of the provincial legislatures. In support of this submission, it will be convenient to indicate briefly

Then they give all the reasons for it. The provinces have acted in that field. There is the Alberta Freedom of Trade Union Association Act. I am pleased to refer to this statute of Alberta, assented to in 1937. It follows the lines of the draft bill proposed by the Trades and Labour Congress, and makes it unlawful for employers to dismiss employees because they are members of or want to remain members of a trade union. It makes the employers liable to a penalty fixed by the act.
The Nova Scotia Trade Union Act, 1937, declares it lawful for employees to form or to join a trade union, and makes it unlawful for employers to prevent them from doing so. In this instance a penalty is fixed by the statute. It is in their field of jurisdiction.
The Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act of British Columbia, 1937, recognizes the right of employers and employees to organize for any lawful [DOT] purposes. There again they make it unlawful to prevent employees from joining a trade union or association, and a penalty is fixed.
The Strikes and Lockouts Prevention Act, 1937, of Manitoba is again, I am sure, the result of the work of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, which has asked those legislatures to act in that way. Manitoba has acted.
Even the province of Quebec has acted, through the Fair Wage Act, 1937, of Quebec. There again we find a penalty for those who try to restrict the freedom of the working man.
In Saskatchewan there is a bill respecting the right of employees to organize. That bill received its first reading on January 28, 1938, and it is still before the legislature. instance, by which it was to be made an indictable offence for any person to solicit or accept any insurance risk, except on behalf of a company or association licensed under the Insurance Act of 1917. . . . their lordships think it is no longer open to dispute that the parliament of Canada cannot, by purporting to create penal sanctions under section 91, head 27, appropriate to itself exclusively a field of jurisdiction in which, apart from such a procedure, it could exert no legal authority, and tliat if. when examined as a whole, legislation in form criminal is found, in aspects and for purposes exclusively within the provincial sphere, to deal with matters committed to the provinces, it cannot be upheld as valid.
In the recent reference to the privy council with respect to section 498A of the criminal code, their lordships said:
The only limitation on the plenary power of the dominion to determine what shall or shall not be criminal is the condition that parliament shall not, in the guise of enacting criminal legislation in truth and in substance, encroach on any of the classes of subjects enumerated in section 92. It is no objection that it does in fact affect them. In a genuine attempt to amend the criminal law it may obviously affect previous existing civil rights.
And further:
In the present case there seems to be no reason for supposing that the dominion are using the criminal law as a pretence or pretext or that the legislation is in pith and substance in any way interfering with civil rights in the province.
They declare the section valid. A similar view in every respect has been expressed by the privy council in other cases. For instance, we have only to refer to the Proprietary Articles Trade Association v. The Attorney General of Canada, reported at 1931 appeal cases, page 324.
In the present bill I think it is obvious from the section, together with the explanatory note, that the proposed legislation is in the guise of criminal legislation for the purpose, in truth and substance, of encroaching upon property and civil rights.
